summary: OAuth 2.0 is the Internet Engineering Task Force framework by which an application obtains limited access to a web service, either with the approval of the person who owns the data or on its own behalf; Request for Comments 6749 defines it and Request for Comments 9728 adds a standard way for a protected service to publish what a client needs to know, such as which authorization servers it trusts and which scope values it accepts. It covers delegation well: scoped, time-limited access tokens, a refresh path, registries for extensions, and discovery of the authorization server for a service the client already knows. It leaves to others the token format, how a service checks tokens with the authorization server, how clients register, how a person is signed in, and everything about the content and behaviour of worlds. A standards audience should know that the framework itself warns it is likely to produce non-interoperable implementations unless profiles fix its optional parts, so saying a system supports OAuth does not tell two systems they will work together. It also authorizes access without authenticating anyone or saying who they are, and its discovery begins only once the client already knows the service address.

coverage.note: An access token denotes a scope and lifetime that the resource server enforces, and the protected resource metadata lists the scope values it accepts, but the token format and how a resource server reads it are left to other specifications.
